result.question: Evaluate the Cactus Compute "Needle" model (https://github.com/cactus-compute/needle, https://huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/needle) as an on-device tool-calling model for Canvas LMS REST API integration. Context: a local-first macOS grading app ("Grader") currently drives Canvas via a CLI tool (canvas-pp-cli) and capped local Ollama models (grader-text:8b, grader-vision:1.3b). The Canvas REST API surface is very large: the instructor's local API doc contains ~417 distinct method+path endpoints, and a Canvas MCP server exposes 646 tools. Questions to answer: (1) What exactly is Needle — architecture, base model, parameter count, context window, tool-calling format, license, and inference requirements? (2) Is it viable to drive a 400-650-tool API surface — what is Needle's documented max tool count per call, its benchmark numbers on tool selection (BFCL or similar), and what tool-count limits do small tool-calling models generally hit? Is a two-stage router (retrieve candidate tools, then call) the standard workaround? (3) Could Needle run locally on Apple Silicon alongside a CLI tool as an intent-to-API-call router — what runtimes does it support (Cactus SDK, GGUF/llama.cpp, Ollama, MLX)? (4) Fine-tuning feasibility: can Needle or its base model be fine-tuned into a Canvas-LMS-specialized tool-calling model — what does Cactus document about fine-tuning, what training data format would be needed, and are there precedents for fine-tuning small models on large API surfaces? Prioritize primary sources: the cactus-compute/needle GitHub repo, the Cactus-Compute/needle HuggingFace model card, Cactus Compute docs/blog, and function-calling benchmark leaderboards.
result.summary: Needle is a 26M-parameter custom "Simple Attention Network" (encoder-decoder, pure attention with no FFN/MLP layers; 12 encoder + 8 decoder layers, d_model=512) distilled from Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite and post-trained on 2B tokens of single-shot function-call data, released MIT-licensed and fully open on Hugging Face — a purpose-built tool-caller, not a general LLM. It emits calls as a JSON array of {name, arguments} objects, consumes tools in OpenAI function-calling format (or a simplified inline schema in its native repo), and runs on Cactus's from-scratch inference engine (Metal backend on Apple Silicon; no documented GGUF/llama.cpp/Ollama/MLX path), reaching ~6000 tok/s prefill and 1200 tok/s decode. Critically for Grader's use case, Needle publishes no BFCL/numeric benchmark, no context-window size, and no documented maximum-tools-per-call limit; it was trained on only 15 consumer-device tool categories (timers, messaging, navigation, smart home), not a large enterprise REST surface — so its ability to drive a 400–650-tool Canvas API out-of-the-box is unproven and, given the tool-selection literature, unlikely. The research literature strongly establishes that all-tools-in-context fails at scale (13.62% accuracy dumping all tools vs 43.13% with retrieval; retrieval precision degrades past ~100 tools; hosted APIs cap at 128 tools and OpenAI recommends ~20), making a two-stage retrieve-then-call router the standard, near-mandatory workaround for a 400–650-tool surface. Fine-tuning is Needle's intended path to a new domain: Cactus documents local Mac/PC fine-tuning via `needle finetune data.jsonl` (or a web UI) using a JSONL dataset with query/tools/answers fields, recommending ≥120 examples per tool (100 train / 10 val / 10 test) to avoid overfitting — which for Canvas implies a substantial synthetic-data generation effort.

findings.claim: Needle is a 26M-parameter custom encoder-decoder 'Simple Attention Network' (pure attention, no FFN/MLP; 12 encoder + 8 decoder layers, d_model=512, GQA 8H/4KV, RoPE, 8192 BPE vocab) distilled from Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite and post-trained on 2B tokens of single-shot function-call data — a purpose-built function-caller, not a general-purpose LLM like Grader's decoder-only Ollama models.
findings.evidence: GitHub repo and HF model card both state verbatim '26m parameter Simple Attention Network', 'Encoder: 12 layers, GQA (8H/4KV), RoPE, gated residuals', 'Decoder: 8 layers, self-attn + cross-attn', 'd_model: 512', 'We distilled Gemini 3.1 into a 26m parameter...', and 'Post-trained on 2B tokens of single-shot function call dataset (45mins)'. Pretraining was '200B tokens on 16x TPU v6e (27hrs)'. Architecture is 'Encoder-decoder, pure attention (no FFN)'. Independent coverage (NYU Shanghai RITS, ai-tldr.dev) confirms distillation from Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite and FFN-free SAN design. The encoder-decoder, MLP-free design is genuinely non-standard vs Grader's decoder-only Llama-family models. Merges claims [0],[4],[7],[9],[13],[15] — all unanimous 3-0.

findings.claim: Needle is released under the MIT license with weights fully open on Hugging Face (Cactus-Compute/needle) and dataset-generation code open — permitting commercial use, modification, and redistribution, which is compatible with embedding it in the Grader product.
findings.evidence: HF README YAML metadata contains authoritative machine-readable 'license: mit'; card body states 'License: MIT'. GitHub README: 'Weights are fully open on Cactus-Compute/needle, as well as the dataset generation.' Cactus blog: 'Everything is MIT licensed.' Corroborated by Gigazine, TechPlanet, NYU RITS, DevPik. Needle is a from-scratch 26M architecture (not a weight-derivative of a restrictively-licensed base), so no upstream base-model license overrides the MIT tag. ONE CAVEAT flagged by verifier: Google's Gemini API ToS may restrict using Gemini outputs to build competing models — a legal question between Cactus and Google about the distillation-data provenance, not a change to Needle's MIT release status, but worth legal review if relicensing cleanliness matters. Merges claims [1],[5].

findings.claim: Needle emits tool calls as a JSON array of {name, arguments} objects and consumes tool definitions in OpenAI function-calling format via the Cactus runtime (`cactus run Cactus-Compute/needle [--tools my_tools.json]`, demo toolset by default); the standalone `needle` repo uses a parallel interface (`needle run --query ... --tools '<inline JSON>'`, plus a `needle playground` Gradio web UI at 127.0.0.1:7860) with a simplified per-parameter-required schema rather than strict OpenAI format.
findings.evidence: Output format confirmed verbatim on both primary sources: [{"name":"get_weather","arguments":{"location":"San Francisco"}}]. Cactus SDK README line 181: 'cactus run Cactus-Compute/needle [--tools my_tools.json]  # OpenAI function-calling format; demo toolset by default'; CLI reference line 232: '--tools <json|file>   tool definitions for tool calling'. NUANCE (verifier-confirmed, not a contradiction): there are two entry points — the Cactus runtime SDK (`cactus run`, file-based --tools, 'OpenAI function-calling format' label, default demo toolset) and the standalone needle training-repo CLI (`needle run`, inline JSON string, no default toolset, simplified schema with per-param 'required' booleans and no type:function wrapper). The 'OpenAI function-calling format' label describes the tool-definition INPUT; the model OUTPUT is the custom {name, arguments} JSON array. Merges claims [1],[6],[14],[15],[16],[17] — five unanimous, note [18] below covers runtime.

findings.claim: Needle's ONLY reported benchmarking is qualitative single-shot function-calling superiority over four other tiny models (FunctionGemma-270M, Qwen-0.6B, Granite-350M, LFM2.5-350M); it publishes NO numeric BFCL score, NO context-window/max-sequence-length, and NO documented maximum tool count per call, and the post concedes those larger models 'have more scope/capacity and excel in conversational settings.'
findings.evidence: All three primary sources contain the verbatim line 'it beats FunctionGemma-270m, Qwen-0.6B, Graninte-350m, LFM2.5-350m on single-shot function call' with zero numbers attached. Blog concedes: 'those models have more scope/capacity and excel in conversational settings.' Three negative sub-claims independently confirmed absent across GitHub, raw README, HF card, and web search: (a) no numeric BFCL/accuracy score for Needle anywhere; (b) no context-window size documented (RoPE and d_model=512 listed but no max sequence length); (c) no maximum-tools-per-call limit documented. This is the single most important gap for the Canvas use case: there is no published evidence Needle can select correctly among hundreds of tools. Merges claims [3],[6],[11] — all unanimous 3-0.

findings.claim: Needle was post-trained only on Gemini-synthesized data covering 15 consumer-device tool categories (timers, messaging, navigation, smart home, etc.), targeting on-device 'personal AI' on phones/watches/glasses — NOT a large enterprise REST API surface — so driving a 400–650-tool Canvas surface is entirely out of its training distribution and unproven without fine-tuning.
findings.evidence: Cactus blog states verbatim: 'Dataset synthesized via Gemini with 15 tool categories (timers, messaging, navigation, smart home, etc.)' and 'Post-trained on 2B tokens of synthesized function-calling data.' GitHub `needle generate-data` command 'Synthesize[s] training data via Gemini'. Corroborated by NYU RITS, DevPik, Gigazine describing consumer/on-device framing. Verifier caveat: only 4 of 15 categories are named ('etc.'), and the 'not an enterprise REST surface / Canvas-relevance' is sound inference rather than a directly-sourced Canvas assertion — but the load-bearing training-data disclosure is exact. This is a limitation the vendor discloses, so no marketing bias. Claim [10], unanimous 3-0.

findings.claim: Needle runs on Cactus's own from-scratch inference engine (C/C++ core with Python, Swift, Kotlin, Flutter, React Native, Rust bindings) targeting mobile/wearables/custom hardware, with a Metal backend on Apple Silicon (macOS/iOS) and ARM NEON CPU kernels — so it CAN run locally on Apple Silicon, but GGUF, llama.cpp, Ollama, and MLX are NOT documented as supported runtimes, meaning there is no documented drop-in path to co-run alongside Grader's existing Ollama stack.
findings.evidence: Blog: 'Cactus, an inference engine built from scratch for mobile, wearables and custom hardware.' Docs enumerate bindings 'Swift, Kotlin, Flutter, React Native, Python, Rust', 'Metal (Apple GPU backend)', platforms macOS/iOS/iPadOS/Android; v1 engine uses proprietary 'Cactus Quants' (4-bit-to-1-bit) format and a PyTorch-to-Cactus-graph transpiler. No GGUF/GGML/llama.cpp/Ollama/MLX references as supported runtimes in current docs or README. IMPORTANT NUANCE: Cactus's separate comparison marketing pages DO advertise GGUF model loading ('Cactus supports GGUF model loading') — so integration alongside a GGUF/Ollama stack is not impossible, it is simply not documented for Needle specifically. The related refuted claim (proprietary 'hybrid edge-cloud' framing, 1-2) and the split vote on [18] (2-1) reflect this GGUF-support ambiguity. For Grader: Needle would most naturally run via the Cactus runtime as a separate process/binding (Python binding available), NOT inside Ollama. Merges claims [12],[18].

findings.claim: Needle supports LOCAL fine-tuning on a Mac/PC — the documented path to specialize it on a new API surface such as Canvas — invoked as `needle finetune data.jsonl` (CLI) or via a Gradio web UI; the training data is JSONL with three fields per line (query, tools, answers), and Cactus recommends AT LEAST 120 examples per tool (100 train / 10 val / 10 test) or the model overfits ('perfect training metrics but the model won't generalize').
findings.evidence: HF card: 'you can even finetune locally on your Mac/PC', 'Finetune on your own tools via the web UI or CLI', command `needle finetune data.jsonl`, 'Web UI (generates data via Gemini, trains, evaluates, bundles result)'. GitHub confirms JSONL format (query / tools JSON-encoded / answers JSON-encoded) and 'Provide at least 120 examples per tool (100 train / 10 val / 10 test). Fewer examples will overfit.' Corroborated by DeepWiki, DevPik, EveryDev.ai, MindStudio. CAVEAT for Grader: the web-UI data-generation step calls the Gemini CLOUD API — only the CLI path with pre-generated local data is fully offline, which matters for Grader's on-device/privacy constraints. For a 400–650-tool Canvas surface, ≥120 examples/tool implies ~50,000–78,000 synthetic training examples — a substantial (but scriptable) data-generation effort. Merges claims [2],[8].

findings.claim: A two-stage retrieve-then-call router is the standard, near-mandatory mitigation for large tool surfaces: dumping all tool descriptions in-context ('Blank Conditioning') yields only 13.62% tool-selection accuracy, whereas retrieving and injecting only the single best tool (RAG-MCP) raises it to 43.13% (a >3x improvement) via semantic search over a tool index before the LLM is invoked.
findings.evidence: RAG-MCP (arXiv:2505.03275v1) Table 1: MCP-RAG 43.13%, Actual Match 18.20%, Blank Conditioning 13.62% (all-N-descriptions-at-once), on the MCPBench web-search subset. Mechanism confirmed: 'A lightweight LLM-based retriever encodes the user's task description and performs a semantic search over the MCP index, returning the top-k candidate MCPs' and 'Only the single best MCP description ... is injected.' Toolshed (arXiv:2410.14594) independently frames the two standard scaling approaches as (1) fine-tuning for tool use and (2) retriever-based selection from a vector DB. CAVEATS: RAG-MCP v1 is a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the winning method's proponents (self-interested), and 43% absolute accuracy is still low — 'effective' holds in the comparative sense. Corroborated directionally by Gorilla, ToolLLM, Toolshed. Merges claims [19],[21],[23]; [23] also names fine-tuning as the alternate scaling path (directly relevant to Needle fine-tuning finding).

findings.claim: Tool-selection reliability degrades once the tool registry grows past roughly 100 tools, and hosted function-calling APIs (OpenAI, Google Gemini 1.5 Pro; per one paper also Anthropic) cap at 128 tool definitions per request, with OpenAI recommending ~20 tools per agent to maintain accuracy — all far below Grader's 400–650-tool Canvas surface, confirming all-tools-in-context is not viable and a retrieval/fine-tuning stage is required.
findings.evidence: RAG-MCP stress test varies N (registry size) from 1 to ~1100/11100 and finds 'beyond position ~100 ... retrieval precision diminishes when handling very large tool registries.' Toolshed (arXiv:2410.14594): 'OpenAI (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), Anthropic (claude-3-5-sonnet), Google Gemini 1.5 Pro support up to 128 tool function definitions in the API request, though OpenAI recommends limiting it to around 20 tools per agent.' 128-tool cap independently verified as a live, current (2025-2026) OpenAI API hard limit ('Invalid tools: array too long. Expected an array with maximum length 128'); ~20-tool recommendation confirmed in OpenAI's function-calling guide. IMPORTANT NUANCE for Grader: the 128 hard cap is an OpenAI/Azure hosted-API artifact — local Ollama/llama.cpp/MLX/Cactus models have NO such API cap, BUT small local tool-callers (like 26M Needle) still degrade well before hundreds of tools, so the retrieval/fine-tuning workaround still applies. One paper's claim that Anthropic also caps at 128 is contradicted by other sources (Anthropic imposes no such hard limit). ToolRet (arXiv:2503.01763, ACL 2025) and reports of degradation as early as 30-50 tools make '~100' conservative. Merges claims [20],[22],[23].
findings.vote: 2-1 on [20] (position-vs-registry-size ambiguity, resolved in claim's favor); [22] unanimous 3-0

result.caveats: TIME-SENSITIVITY: Needle is a very recent release (~May 2026) and all vendor claims (speeds, benchmark superiority, architecture) are ~2 months old as of this research (July 2026); figures may shift and no independent third-party benchmark of Needle existed at research time. VENDOR-REPORTED, UNVERIFIED NUMBERS: the 6000 tok/s prefill / 1200 tok/s decode speeds are Cactus-reported on unspecified hardware; the 'beats FunctionGemma/Qwen/Granite/LFM2.5' claim has ZERO published numbers behind it and comes from the vendor's own blog/repo. NO BFCL SCORE EXISTS for Needle — any accuracy expectation for Canvas is pure extrapolation. THE CENTRAL UNKNOWN: Needle documents no maximum-tools-per-call and no context window, and was trained on only 15 consumer tool categories — there is no evidence, positive or negative, about how it behaves with 400-650 heterogeneous Canvas tools; the tool-selection literature (13.62% all-tools accuracy, ~100-tool degradation threshold) strongly suggests it would fail badly without a retrieval front-end or heavy fine-tuning. SOURCE QUALITY: the two-stage-router evidence rests substantially on RAG-MCP (arXiv:2505.03275v1), a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the method's own proponents with low absolute accuracy (43%); the directional finding (retrieval beats tool-stuffing) is well-corroborated but the specific percentages are self-interested. RUNTIME INTEGRATION is documented only for Cactus's own engine; GGUF/Ollama co-running is advertised generically on Cactus marketing pages but NOT documented for Needle specifically (this drove the one split vote, [18] at 2-1, and the one refuted claim). GEMINI-DISTILLATION ToS: MIT release is confirmed, but the upstream question of whether Gemini's API terms permit using its outputs to train a redistributable competing model is unresolved and is a legal matter, not covered by the sources. TWO CLI INTERFACES exist (`cactus run` SDK vs standalone `needle` repo) with different tool-schema conventions — integration work must target the right one.
openQuestions: Fine-tuned on a Canvas-specific tool set, what tool-selection accuracy does Needle actually achieve — and does 26M parameters have enough capacity to reliably discriminate among 400-650 tools, or does it hit the small-model tool-count ceiling regardless of fine-tuning? (No published evidence exists either way; would require an empirical fine-tune-and-benchmark.)

What is Needle's actual maximum context window / input token limit, and how many tool definitions can physically fit in one call? The architecture uses RoPE and d_model=512 but no max sequence length is documented anywhere — this directly bounds whether even a retrieved top-k subset fits.

Can the Cactus runtime realistically co-exist with Grader's Ollama stack on the same Mac (memory, process model, Metal contention), and is there a supported GGUF/Ollama export path for Needle specifically, or must Grader adopt the Cactus SDK (Python binding) as a second inference runtime?

Does using Gemini-distilled outputs to fine-tune and redistribute a Canvas-specialized Needle create any licensing/ToS exposure under Google's Gemini API terms, given Grader is a commercial product — and does the fully-offline requirement rule out Cactus's Gemini-cloud-backed web-UI data-generation path, forcing a custom local synthetic-data pipeline for the ~50k-78k Canvas training examples implied by ≥120 examples/tool?

refuted.claim: Cactus is a proprietary on-device inference engine ('hybrid edge-cloud AI engine for mobile devices & wearables') that ships its own runtime with native bindings (Swift, Kotlin, Flutter, React Native, Python, Rust) rather than running on llama.cpp, GGUF, MLX, or Ollama.
